strengths: Novel and reasonably well-motivated hybrid Gaussian-particle framework that couples MPM physical simulation with 3D Gaussian Splatting to add dynamic global weather effects (snow, rain, fog, sandstorm) as well as falling/landing rigid objects to static reconstructed scenes.

The three-stage pipeline (Gaussian-to-particle mapping, MPM simulation with a mesh-derived static particle set, particle-to-Gaussian re-rendering with effect-specific appearance and collision handling) is a sensible and technically coherent design that allows dynamic elements to interact with existing scene geometry, addressing a real limitation of prior single-object physics-based Gaussian animation and of purely static weather-compositing methods (e.g., ClimateNeRF).

Effect-specific collision handling (surface projection for snow/sand, a volumetric wetness grid with temporal decay for rain) is a concrete and demonstrated technical contribution, supported by a clear ablation (Figure 7) showing qualitative benefit versus a no-collision-handling variant.

Reasonably broad qualitative demonstration across five scenes (Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks & Temples) and multiple effect types, plus extension to object-level dynamics (falling leaves/feathers, landing drone/bee), and a controllability study (Figure 4) showing tunable fog color, sand scale, and snow quantity.

Good reproducibility support: detailed appendix specifying MPM material parameters, grid resolution, particle emission rates, rendering scale/opacity/color settings per effect, and links/settings for baseline reproduction.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparisons (Table 1) are against static 3D editing methods (ClimateNeRF, GaussCtrl) that are not designed to produce dynamic, temporally evolving effects; this is an inherently favorable and somewhat unfair comparison for demonstrating 'state-of-the-art' dynamic weather synthesis, since the baselines cannot represent motion at all. No quantitative comparison is made against more directly relevant dynamic/physics-based methods mentioned in related work (e.g., PhysGaussian, Gaussian Splashing, or the concurrent RainyGS), even though RainyGS is explicitly acknowledged as tackling the same rain-effect problem.

The evaluation metrics used (CLIP similarity, CLIP direction similarity, VQAScore) are single-frame, semantic/text-alignment proxies borrowed from text-guided editing evaluation; they do not directly measure temporal coherence, physical plausibility of motion, or realism of dynamics, which are the paper's central claims ('physically plausible motion', 'significantly outperforms ... in physical realism'). No physics-grounded metric, temporal-consistency metric (e.g., optical-flow or video-based FVD), or user study is provided to substantiate these claims.

Evaluation breadth is limited to five scenes total and effects are demonstrated mostly qualitatively (Figures 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10); there is no systematic per-effect quantitative table across all five scenes, and only one ablation figure (qualitative, no numeric ablation metrics) is given for collision handling.

Interaction is explicitly one-directional: dynamic particles react to the static scene, but the static scene cannot be deformed or moved by the dynamic effects, which the authors acknowledge but which limits the realism of e.g. heavy sandstorm or debris interactions.

Appearance parameters are largely hand-tuned per effect and per scene (extensive manually chosen scale/opacity/color/velocity constants listed in the appendix), raising concerns about generalization to new scenes/effects without significant manual re-tuning, which the authors themselves list as a limitation.

Runtime is reported only as a single aggregate number (7 FPS on an RTX A5000) without characterizing how it scales with particle count, effect type, or scene complexity, leaving practical usability and scalability to more particles/longer sequences unclear.

Mesh extraction and the reliance on TSDF fusion for collision geometry could introduce failure modes in thin or complex structures (e.g., foliage, bicycles) that are not explicitly analyzed; the paper does not discuss failure cases or robustness limits of the mesh-based collision approach.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: introducing dynamic, physically-simulated global weather effects (snow, rain, fog, sandstorm) into static 3DGS scenes, going beyond single-object animation.

The three-stage Gaussian-to-particle-to-Gaussian pipeline with MPM simulation and mesh-based collision handling is a reasonable engineering combination that allows dynamic particles to interact with pre-reconstructed static scene geometry.

Demonstrates versatility across multiple scenes (Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples) and multiple effect types, as well as extensions to falling/landing rigid objects (leaves, feathers, drones), showing some generality of the framework.

Provides reasonably detailed implementation/appendix information (MPM parameters, collision-handling specifics per effect, mesh extraction procedure), which aids reproducibility of the described pipeline.
Includes an ablation showing the qualitative benefit of the proposed collision-handling component over a no-collision-handling baseline.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation is very thin: Table 1 only reports CLIP similarity/direction and VQAScore against two baselines (ClimateNeRF, GaussCtrl) that are static text-driven 3D editing methods, not physics-based dynamic weather simulators; this is an apples-to-oranges comparison that does not actually measure the paper's central claim of physically plausible *dynamic* motion (no temporal consistency, no motion/physics-fidelity metric, no FVD, no user study on realism or motion plausibility).

No quantitative or qualitative comparison to the most relevant concurrent method, RainyGS, which also targets dynamic weather on Gaussian scenes; the paper only distinguishes itself from RainyGS in text without any experimental comparison.

AutoVFX comparison is qualitative only and is somewhat straw-manned (the paper states AutoVFX 'cannot' handle these cases rather than running a fair, matched comparison), and no comparison at all is made to other physics-coupled 3DGS works mentioned in related work (PhysGaussian, Feature Splatting, PAC-NeRF, VR-GS) despite the method building directly on their machinery (e.g., the rotation-tracking scheme is explicitly borrowed from PhysGaussian/Feature Splatting).

Appearance parameters for each effect are manually hand-tuned per scene/effect (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation), raising concerns about generalizability, scalability to new scenes, and the degree of human engineering required behind seemingly automated results; this also makes the 'controllability' claims less convincing as true physical controllability versus manual art-direction.

Technical novelty is limited: the core components (3DGS, mesh extraction via TSDF per 2DGS, MPM simulation via Taichi/Feature-Splatting codebase, GaussianDreamer for object appearance) are all existing techniques; the contribution is primarily integration engineering (particle mapping, surface-projection/wetness-grid heuristics for collision) rather than a new simulation or representation method, and these heuristics (surface-offset snow accumulation, exponential-decay wetness grid, anisotropic sand scaling) are ad hoc rather than physically derived or validated against real reference data.

No failure-case analysis beyond a brief, generic limitations paragraph (unidirectional scene-to-particle coupling, manual appearance tuning); no discussion of simulation stability, grid-resolution sensitivity, or runtime/quality trade-offs beyond a single reported FPS number.

Figures such as rainfall results are hard to assess even with zoomed insets, and the paper relies heavily on a project webpage for video evidence, which cannot be verified in the static manuscript; this limits the reviewer's ability to assess the core claim of 'dynamic' and 'physically plausible' motion from the paper alone.

The evaluation covers a small number of scenes (5) with effects applied in isolation per scene; there is no systematic study of robustness across diverse/more cluttered scenes, varying effect intensities, or longer time horizons, limiting evidence for generality.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: prior physics+3DGS/NeRF work largely animates single existing objects, while this paper targets scene-wide dynamic weather effects (snow, rain, fog, sandstorm) that interact with complex static geometry.

Technically coherent three-stage pipeline (Gaussian→particle mapping via mesh extraction, MPM-based simulation with stationary particles for the static scene, particle→Gaussian mapping with effect-specific appearance and collision handling) is clearly motivated and well described.

Effect-specific collision handling (surface projection for snow/sand, a wetness grid for rain) is a sensible, practical solution to the coarse-grid MPM limitation, and the ablation (Fig. 7) shows it visibly improves realistic accumulation versus no collision handling.

Qualitative results across five diverse real scenes (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks and Temples) and multiple effects look visually convincing, and the method also generalizes to falling/landing object effects (leaves, feathers, drones), demonstrating some versatility beyond weather.
Reasonable comparisons to related static-editing methods (ClimateNeRF, GaussCtrl) and to AutoVFX for single-object insertion show qualitative and CLIP/VQAScore-based quantitative advantages.
Extensive appendix with implementation and per-effect parameter details (material constants, particle counts, grid resolution, rendering parameters) supports reproducibility.
Controllability over parameters (fog color, sand scale, snow quantity) is demonstrated, which is useful for practical content-creation applications.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation relies solely on CLIP similarity/direction and VQAScore, metrics designed for text-driven image editing assessment, not for judging temporal dynamics, physical plausibility, or video-level realism, which are the paper's central claims; no video-based metrics (e.g., FVD), temporal-consistency measure, or user study is reported.

The main quantitative baselines (ClimateNeRF, GaussCtrl) are static editing methods not designed to model dynamics, so the comparison mostly shows that a dynamic method looks better than a static one on CLIP-type metrics, which is not a strong test of the paper's specific technical contributions (MPM simulation, collision handling).

The closely related concurrent method RainyGS is discussed in related work but never compared against, even qualitatively, leaving the paper's advantage over the most directly comparable existing approach untested.

Appearance and physical parameters (Young's modulus, Poisson ratio, particle counts, colors, scales, wetness decay rates, etc.) are manually hand-tuned per effect (and implicitly per scene, given the case-specific values in Appendix A.3), which raises concerns about generality/automation and the amount of manual effort needed to apply the method to a new scene — a limitation the paper itself partly acknowledges but does not quantify.

Evaluation breadth is limited: five scenes and four main weather effects (plus a handful of object-insertion demos), with no failure-case analysis beyond a short qualitative limitations discussion, and no assessment of scaling to larger or more complex scenes.

The MPM simulation runs on a coarse 64^3 grid, necessitating ad hoc collision-handling workarounds rather than resolving the underlying resolution limitation; how this affects fidelity for larger scenes or finer effects (e.g., dense rain) is not analyzed.
No discussion of overall computational cost (mesh extraction + MPM simulation time) beyond a single rendering-speed figure (7 FPS), leaving reproducibility of end-to-end runtime unclear.

The framework only supports one-directional interaction (dynamic elements respond to the static scene, but the static scene cannot be deformed/moved by the dynamic effects), a real physical limitation acknowledged only briefly as future work.
